newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb opposition calls for bigger demonstrations.
newsitem.headline: Serb opposition calls for bigger demonstrations.

text.p: The Serbian opposition called for a huge anti-government demonstration on Saturday while ruling Socialists indicated they were still fighting against the restoration of November's annulled election results.

"Tomorrow we must stage a mass protest to mark these two months (of protests) and face the police in our own uniforms --- army reserve, civil defence, doctors, stewardesses, every possible uniform," Vuk Draskovic, a leader of the Zajedno (Together) coalition, said the 61st day of protests on Friday.
The coalition and its student allies are protesting to overturn the government's annulment of Zajedno victories in 14 of Serbia's major cities in November 17 municipal elections.

With numbers of demonstrators down sharply to a daily average of 15,000 to 20,000 in Belgrade, the opposition leaders said it was time for another big rally approaching in size the half-million who turned out on Orthodox New Year.

Up to 400 students spent all night at a rally in central Belgrade because a police cordon prevented them from marching through the city. They said they would stay there until the police allowed them to march.
Witnesses said the mood was friendly between the students and the police and there were no incidents.
The opposition said a court in Serbia's second-biggest city of Nis had rejected a Socialist Party (SPS) challenge to an electoral commission ruling restoring the opposition's victory there.
"The court ruled that the Socialist Party's appeal was unfounded," Zoran Zivkovic, the local Zajedno leader, said by telephone on Friday.
Earlier this week, electoral commissions in Nis and Belgrade ruled that the opposition victories there were valid.

But Ratko Markovic, a Belgrade University law professor and member of the SPS executive board, said in a statement read on state-run Serbian television that the reasoning behind the electoral commission decisions was deeply flawed.
Markovic said electoral commissions had no legal authority to overturn court decisions, and therefore the court rulings which threw out the Zajedno victories for "irregularities" remained in effect.
"All in all, the decision of the municipal electoral commission is a nightmare of legal nonsense, illegalities and fallacies," Markovic said in the statement read during the evening news broadcast.

"It's as if someone went to pains to put everything upside down -- the administration controls the legality of the court...The decision is thus a legal monstrosity that could only have been thought up by someone who wanted to ridicule the law."

Socialist hardliners have vowed to challenge the pro-opposition ruling in Belgrade, snubbing a plea from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) to concede electoral defeat in the 14 towns.

But the persistent mass demonstrations by Zajedno and allied university students have rattled the foundations of the left's effective one-party rule stretching back to 1945 and brought international celebrity to the opposition leaders.

Zajedno leaders Draskovic, Vesna Pesic and Zoran Djindjic returned on Friday from consultations in Italy with Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini. It was announced immediately afterwards that Djindjic was flying to Bonn this weekend to meet German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel.
Dusan Vasiljevic, a student protest leader, will attend U.S. President Bill Clinton's inauguration in Washington on Monday, a U.S. embassy official confirmed.
Vasiljevic is going to Washington as a guest of Milan Panic, the Yugoslav-born businessman who made a fortune in pharmaceuticals in the United States and served as Yugoslav prime minister in 1992.
